claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has an FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy is uniform and has minimal elemental segregation.
Selective oxidation of key constituent elements governs degradation during elevated-temperature gas exposure.
Under oxidizing conditions, Cr and Ti diffuse or segregate preferentially to the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched Cr and Ti react with oxygen to form a Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale.
The Cr/Ti-rich scale formed under oxidizing conditions is thin, continuous, and adherent.
A continuous Cr/Ti-rich scale passivates the surface and reduces subsequent degradation.
Lower oxygen activity under reducing conditions hampers formation of the protective Cr/Ti-rich scale.
Reducing conditions produce discontinuous, porous, Al-rich oxides.
The Al-rich oxide layer produced under reducing conditions is thicker than the oxide layer produced under oxidizing conditions.
The porous Al-rich oxide formed under reducing conditions causes faster and more pronounced surface degradation.
Differences in oxide composition, continuity, and adherence control the surface degradation rate.
The underlying FCC matrix remains largely intact despite the predicted differences in surface oxidation.
Bulk strength and fatigue performance remain relatively preserved after the proposed exposures.
The as-manufactured baseline exhibits balanced strength and fatigue performance.
The proposed comparison exposes identical specimens at 800–1000°C under oxygen-rich and hydrogen- or carbon-monoxide-rich atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply at 800–1000°C when the compared gases have substantially different oxygen partial pressures.
Similar oxide-scale characteristics and degradation rates in the oxidizing and reducing conditions would falsify the selective-oxidation hypothesis.
